title: Learning Through Talk: If Talking Helps Learning, That Means Everyone Needs to Talk eryone-needs-to-talk/
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington, writing ahead of the Voice 21 Great Oracy exhibition, argues that talk is fundamental to learning and not an extra. Using the memory and learning model from his WalkThrus work, he explains how explaining an idea aloud forces attention, selection and organization, retrieval, elaboration and the testing of ideas against an audience. Having to turn a non-linear schema into a linear spoken account exposes gaps in knowledge that prompt further learning, and the more students practise talking through a domain, the more fluent they become. If talk helps one person, he says, it should help everyone, which is why he favors routines such as Practise Explaining over cold calls or choral responses that involve only a few students. He cites Belgian research by Speltincx and Vanhoof listing benefits of an everyone-speaks principle: more learning, engagement, belonging and better relationships, with less disruption.
points: Talk supports learning because it requires attention, selection and organization of ideas, retrieval of prior knowledge and elaboration.
Turning a web of connected ideas into a linear explanation reveals gaps in understanding that students can then work to close.
If talk helps one student, every student should have the chance to explain, which makes whole-class routines like Practise Explaining better than a few cold calls.
Speltincx and Vanhoof report that paired discussion brings more learning and engagement, better relationships, a stronger sense of belonging and less problematic behavior.
Routine talk with the right resources gives students something to think with and builds their agency as learners.
quotes: Talk requires attention – you can’t talk unless your attention is on the ideas you’re talking about.
Talk demands thinking, it requires selecting and organising ideas – the core of generative learning.
Sometimes we hesitate, stop and start and rephrase things, hearing our own ideas take shape as we talk them through.
It’s the interaction with this external audience that helps ideas to surface, to be open to examination in comparison to other sets of ideas.
Why would you only want a small subset of students to have the opportunity to explain a concept when you could easily set it up so that they all can?

Underpinning this: the amount of time students spend talking about the content is a determining factor in their results, and structures that let everyone join the discussion raise both the participation and the attainment of students from disadvantaged groups.
Once you make talk absolutely routine, engaging all students systematically, supported by the resources needed to stimulate productive knowledge-building, the learning benefits are significant.
